Spring
spring
n. and v.i. (a source of water rising from the ground; to leap up or issue forth; rendering Hebrew mayan, maqor, Greek pege, hallomai)
Old English springan, to leap. The noun and verb are one word because a spring is water that leaps — and the Lord Jesus keeps the verbal force when He describes water “springing up into everlasting life.”

Biblical Definition

A spring is living water rising of itself, as opposed to a cistern which only holds what is poured in, and Scripture builds a whole doctrine on the difference. Jeremiah's indictment turns on it: Israel has committed two evils, forsaking the fountain of living waters and hewing out broken cisterns that can hold no water (Jeremiah 2:13). The Lord Jesus makes the promise correspondingly interior: “the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life” (John 4:14) — not a reservoir the believer must keep refilling but a source placed within him, which is the Spirit. Solomon uses the image for the moral consequences of a righteous man's collapse: “A righteous man falling down before the wicked is as a troubled fountain, and a corrupt spring” (Proverbs 25:26) — the damage is not private, because a fouled spring poisons everyone downstream, which is why the failure of a godly man is a public disaster. James applies the same physics to the tongue: “Doth a fountain send forth at the same place sweet water and bitter?” (James 3:11). The question expects no, and the argument is that speech reveals a source. A man does not have a blessing-spring and a cursing-spring; he has one, and what comes out identifies it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Water rising of itself, against the cistern which merely holds. Christ promises a spring placed within the believer; Solomon says a righteous man's fall fouls a public source; James argues that one fountain cannot yield sweet and bitter.

expand to see more

SPRING, v.i. [Sax. springan.] To vegetate and rise out of the ground; to begin to appear; as, the corn springs.

2. To issue or proceed, as from a source; as, water springs from a fountain.

3. To leap; to bound; to jump.

SPRING, n. A leap; a bound; a jump.

6. A fountain of water; an issue of water from the earth, or the basin of water at the place of its issue.

Key Scripture

John 4:14 — "But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life."

Proverbs 25:26 — "A righteous man falling down before the wicked is as a troubled fountain, and a corrupt spring."

James 3:11 — "Doth a fountain send forth at the same place sweet water and bitter?"

Isaiah 41:18 — "I will open rivers in high places, and fountains in the midst of the valleys: I will make the wilderness a pool of water, and the dry land springs of water."

Modern Corruption

John 4:14 is enlisted for a religion of inner resources — the divine spark, the true self, the wellspring within — when the entire clause depends on the water that I shall give him, a gift from outside that the man did not possess.

expand to see more

The line about a well springing up within is a favourite of every spirituality that locates salvation in the self: look inward, the answer is already there, drink from your own depths. The verse says the reverse in its own grammar. Twice in one sentence the Lord Jesus says the water that I shall give him; the spring is inside the man because Christ put it there, and before He put it there the woman had nothing but a bucket and a well that ran dry every day. This is precisely the Reformed doctrine of regeneration — a new principle of life implanted by the Spirit, not a latent capacity awakened. The interiority of the gift is real and glorious, and it is not native. Jeremiah 2:13 supplies the alternative on offer: a man who will not have the fountain does not thereby have nothing, he has cisterns of his own making, and they leak.

Proverbs 25:26 speaks to a second and more painful corruption, the modern instinct to treat a leader's fall as his own affair. Solomon calls the righteous man who gives way before the wicked a fouled spring, and the metaphor is chosen for its scope: a spring serves a town. When a man who has taught the truth abandons it under pressure, everyone who drank from him is affected, which is why Scripture holds teachers to a stricter judgment (James 3:1) and why the qualifications for elders are so heavily weighted toward character. The point is not that his sin is worse in kind; it is that his position makes it public water.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew mayan (a spring, fountain) and maqor (a source, wellspring — used of the heart in Proverbs 4:23); Greek pege (a spring or fountain) and hallomai (to leap, the verb in John 4:14).

expand to see more

Hebrew mayan (H4599) — a spring, fountain; used of literal springs and of the fountain of Israel in Psalm 68:26.

Hebrew maqor (H4726) — a source, wellspring; used in Proverbs 4:23 of the heart, out of which are the issues of life.

Hebrew mabbua (H4002) — a bubbling spring; the word in Isaiah 35:7 and 49:10.

Greek pege (G4077) — a spring, fountain; the noun in John 4:14 and James 3:11, and used of the fountain of the water of life in Revelation 21:6.

Greek hallomai (G242) — to leap, spring up; the vivid verb in John 4:14, elsewhere used of the lame man leaping in Acts 3:8.

Usage

"“The water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water” — interior, and given; never native."

"“A troubled fountain, and a corrupt spring” — a righteous man's collapse fouls a public source."

"“Doth a fountain send forth at the same place sweet water and bitter?” — speech identifies the source it came from."
